summary.text: Lucas congruences modulo \(3\) give \(A(3m),A(3m+1),A(3m+2)\equiv A(m),-A(m),A(m)\), while parity of the binomial sum makes every \(A(m)\) odd; hence adjacent terms sum to a multiple of \(6\), and adding each preceding Hankel row to the next shows the determinant is divisible by \(6^n\), yielding \(16\cdot3^n\) divisibility for \(n\ge4\) with the three smaller positive cases computed directly. Thus the scaled series is \(1+16Y\), and an integral eighth root is constructed coefficient-by-coefficient: roots with even positive-degree coefficients have eighth powers whose positive-degree coefficients are divisible by \(16\), so each new coefficient can cancel the residual term after division by \(8\) while remaining even.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
u_n=\sum_{k=0}^n \binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^2
\]
be the Apéry number sequence A005259, and let
\[
h_n=\left|\det (u_{i+j})_{0\leq i,j\leq n}\right|.
\]
Thus \((h_n)_{n\geq0}\) is A228143. We prove that there is a series \(C(x)\in\mathbb Z[[x]]\) such that
\[
C(x)^8=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{h_n}{3^n}x^n
\]
in \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\). Since \(C(0)=1\), this says precisely that the eighth root with constant term \(1\) has integer coefficients.

We divide the proof into four parts.

## 1. Every Apéry number \(u_n\) is odd

We first show that for every \(k>0\),
\[
\binom nk\binom{n+k}{k}
\]
is even. If \(k>n\), the first binomial coefficient is zero, so this is immediate. Suppose that \(k\leq n\). The elementary binomial identity
\[
\binom nk\binom{n+k}{k}
 =\binom{n+k}{2k}\binom{2k}{k}
\]
follows by writing both sides in factorial form.

For \(k>0\), the central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2k}{k}\) is even. Indeed, writing \(k=t+1\), Pascal's identity and symmetry give
\[
\binom{2t+2}{t+1}
 =\binom{2t+1}{t}+\binom{2t+1}{t+1}
 =2\binom{2t+1}{t}.
\]
Consequently \(\binom nk\binom{n+k}{k}\) is even whenever \(k>0\). Hence
\[
\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^2
 =\left(\binom nk\binom{n+k}{k}\right)^2
\]
is even for every \(k>0\). The term with \(k=0\) is \(1\). Therefore
\[
u_n=1+\sum_{k=1}^n\left(\binom nk\binom{n+k}{k}\right)^2
\]
is odd for every \(n\).

## 2. Adjacent Apéry numbers have sum divisible by \(3\)

Put
\[
T(n,k)=\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^2,
\qquad u_n=\sum_{k=0}^nT(n,k).
\]
We use the one-digit form of Lucas's congruence modulo \(3\):
\[
\binom Nk\equiv
\binom{N\bmod 3}{k\bmod 3}
\binom{\lfloor N/3\rfloor}{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}
\pmod 3.
\]
This form follows, for example, by comparing coefficients in
\((1+X)^N=(1+X)^{N\bmod3}((1+X)^3)^{\lfloor N/3\rfloor}\) and using
\((1+X)^3\equiv1+X^3\pmod3\).

We derive three recurrences for \(u_n\) modulo \(3\).

### The case \(n=3m+1\)

Write \(k=3q+s\), where \(s\in\{0,1,2\}\).

If \(s=0\), Lucas's congruence gives
\[
\binom{3m+1}{3q}\equiv\binom mq,
\qquad
\binom{3m+1+3q}{3q}
 =\binom{3(m+q)+1}{3q}
 \equiv\binom{m+q}{q}.
\]
Thus
\[
T(3m+1,3q)\equiv T(m,q)\pmod3.
\]

If \(s=1\), then
\[
\binom{3m+1}{3q+1}\equiv\binom mq,
\]
while
\[
\binom{3m+1+(3q+1)}{3q+1}
 =\binom{3(m+q)+2}{3q+1}
 \equiv \binom21\binom{m+q}{q}
 =2\binom{m+q}{q}.
\]
Because this factor is squared in \(T\), and \(2^2\equiv1\pmod3\), we again obtain
\[
T(3m+1,3q+1)\equiv T(m,q)\pmod3.
\]

If \(s=2\), then
\[
\binom{3m+1}{3q+2}\equiv \binom12\binom mq=0,
\]
so
\[
T(3m+1,3q+2)\equiv0\pmod3.
\]

As \(k\) runs from \(0\) to \(3m+1\), the residue classes \(0\) and \(1\) each correspond to \(q=0,\ldots,m\), while the residue-2 terms vanish. Therefore
\[
u_{3m+1}\equiv 2\sum_{q=0}^mT(m,q)=2u_m\equiv-u_m\pmod3.
\]

### The case \(n=3m+2\)

For \(k=3q\), Lucas's congruence gives
\[
\binom{3m+2}{3q}\equiv\binom mq,
\qquad
\binom{3m+2+3q}{3q}
 =\binom{3(m+q)+2}{3q}
 \equiv\binom{m+q}{q},
\]
and hence
\[
T(3m+2,3q)\equiv T(m,q)\pmod3.
\]

For \(k=3q+1\), the second binomial coefficient is
\[
\binom{3m+2+(3q+1)}{3q+1}
 =\binom{3(m+q+1)}{3q+1},
\]
which is \(0\pmod3\), since its lowest base-3 digit contributes \(\binom01=0\).
For \(k=3q+2\), that second coefficient is
\[
\binom{3m+2+(3q+2)}{3q+2}
 =\binom{3(m+q+1)+1}{3q+2},
\]
which is also \(0\pmod3\), since its lowest digit contributes \(\binom12=0\). Thus only the terms \(k=3q\) survive. Here \(q=0,\ldots,m\), so
\[
u_{3m+2}\equiv\sum_{q=0}^mT(m,q)=u_m\pmod3.
\]

### The case \(n=3m\)

Lucas's congruence gives
\[
\binom{3m}{k}\equiv0\pmod3
\]
unless \(3\mid k\). For \(k=3q\),
\[
\binom{3m}{3q}\equiv\binom mq,
\qquad
\binom{3m+3q}{3q}
 =\binom{3(m+q)}{3q}
 \equiv\binom{m+q}{q}.
\]
Therefore
\[
T(3m,3q)\equiv T(m,q)\pmod3,
\]
and summing over \(q=0,\ldots,m\) gives
\[
u_{3m}\equiv u_m\pmod3.
\]

We now prove, by strong induction on \(n\), that
\[
u_n+u_{n+1}\equiv0\pmod3. \tag{1}
\]
There are three cases according to the residue of \(n\) modulo \(3\).

* If \(n=3m\), then
  \[
  u_n+u_{n+1}=u_{3m}+u_{3m+1}
  \equiv u_m-u_m=0\pmod3.
  \]

* If \(n=3m+1\), then
  \[
  u_n+u_{n+1}=u_{3m+1}+u_{3m+2}
  \equiv-u_m+u_m=0\pmod3.
  \]

* If \(n=3m+2\), then \(n+1=3(m+1)\), and hence
  \[
  u_n+u_{n+1}=u_{3m+2}+u_{3(m+1)}
  \equiv u_m+u_{m+1}\pmod3.
  \]
  Since \(m<3m+2=n\), the last sum is zero by the induction hypothesis.

This proves (1), so \(3\mid u_n+u_{n+1}\) for every \(n\). Since every \(u_n\) is odd, \(u_n+u_{n+1}\) is also divisible by \(2\). The integers \(2\) and \(3\) are coprime, and therefore
\[
6\mid u_n+u_{n+1}\qquad(n\geq0). \tag{2}
\]

## 3. Divisibility of the Hankel determinants

Fix \(N\geq1\), and let
\[
M_N=(u_{i+j})_{0\leq i,j\leq N}.
\]
Starting from the bottom row and proceeding upward, or equivalently multiplying on the left by the lower unitriangular matrix having \(1\)'s on the diagonal and immediately below the diagonal, replace each row \(i>0\) by
\[
\text{row}_i+\text{row}_{i-1}.
\]
Call the resulting matrix \(R_N\). The row-operation matrix is lower triangular with every diagonal entry equal to \(1\), so its determinant is \(1\). Consequently
\[
\det R_N=\det M_N. \tag{3}
\]

For \(i>0\), the \((i,j)\)-entry of \(R_N\) is
\[
u_{i+j}+u_{i-1+j}.
\]
These are adjacent Apéry numbers, so (2) shows that every entry in each of the last \(N\) rows is divisible by \(6\). Factoring a \(6\) from each of these rows gives
\[
6^N\mid\det R_N=\det M_N. \tag{4}
\]
This argument does not depend on the sign of the determinant, so it also gives \(6^N\mid h_N\).

For \(N\geq4\),
\[
6^N=2^N3^N=(16\cdot3^N)2^{N-4},
\]
and therefore (4) implies
\[
16\cdot3^N\mid h_N\qquad(N\geq4). \tag{5}
\]

It remains to cover the three positive indices below \(4\). The needed Apéry numbers, obtained directly from their defining finite sums, are
\[
u_0=1,\quad u_1=5,\quad u_2=73,\quad u_3=1445,
\quad u_4=33001,\quad u_5=819005,\quad u_6=21460825.
\]
Thus the relevant determinants are
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}1&5\\5&73\end{pmatrix}=48,
\]
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
1&5&73\\
5&73&1445\\
73&1445&33001
\end{pmatrix}=161856,
\]
and
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
1&5&73&1445\\
5&73&1445&33001\\
73&1445&33001&819005\\
1445&33001&819005&21460825
\end{pmatrix}=39002646528.
\]
Their respective quotients by \(16\cdot3^N\) are
\[
1,\qquad1124,\qquad90283904,
\]
all integers. Therefore, combining these calculations with (5),
\[
16\cdot3^n\mid h_n\qquad\text{for every }n>0. \tag{6}
\]
Also, the size-one Hankel determinant is
\[
h_0=|u_0|=1. \tag{7}
\]

It follows from (6) that, for \(n>0\), the integer
\[
d_n=\frac{h_n}{16\cdot3^n}
\]
is well defined. Set \(d_0=0\). Equations (6) and (7) show that the scaled Hankel generating series has the form
\[
\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{h_n}{3^n}x^n
 =1+16\sum_{n\geq1}d_nx^n. \tag{8}
\]

## 4. Every series of the form \(1+16D(x)\) is an eighth power over \(\mathbb Z\)

We prove the following general fact.

**Root lemma.** For every sequence of integers \((d_n)_{n\geq1}\), there is a series
\[
C(x)=1+\sum_{n\geq1}c_nx^n\in\mathbb Z[[x]]
\]
such that
\[
C(x)^8=1+16\sum_{n\geq1}d_nx^n. \tag{9}
\]
Moreover, all \(c_n\) with \(n>0\) are even.

We construct the coefficients recursively. Put \(c_0=1\). Suppose that \(c_1,\ldots,c_{r-1}\) have already been defined, and write
\[
P_r(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}c_kx^k,
\qquad e_r=[x^r]P_r(x)^8.
\]
We will show inductively that \(16\mid e_r\), and then define
\[
c_r=\frac{16d_r-e_r}{8}. \tag{10}
\]
The divisibility by \(16\) makes the right side an integer and in fact an even integer.

To justify the required divisibility, suppose inductively that every previously constructed positive-degree coefficient \(c_k\), \(0<k<r\), is even. Since \(c_0=1\), there is then an integral polynomial or power series \(E_r(x)\) such that
\[
P_r(x)=1+2E_r(x).
\]
The binomial expansion can be grouped as
\[
(1+2E)^8
=1+16\bigl(E+7E^2+28E^3+70E^4+112E^5
             +112E^6+64E^7+16E^8\bigr). \tag{11}
\]
Thus every positive-degree coefficient of \((1+2E)^8\) is divisible by \(16\). In particular \(16\mid e_r\). Say \(e_r=16z_r\). Formula (10) then becomes
\[
c_r=\frac{16d_r-16z_r}{8}=2(d_r-z_r),
\]
which is an even integer. This completes the induction and constructs all coefficients \(c_r\).

It remains to prove that the resulting infinite series has the required eighth power. Fix \(r>0\). The coefficient of degree \(r\) in a power of a series depends only on coefficients through degree \(r\). Hence
\[
[x^r]C(x)^8=[x^r](P_r(x)+c_rx^r)^8.
\]
In the binomial expansion, every term containing at least two factors \(c_rx^r\) has degree at least \(2r>r\), so it makes no contribution to degree \(r\). The term containing exactly one such factor contributes
\[
8c_r[x^0]P_r(x)^7=8c_r,
\]
because \(P_r(0)=c_0=1\). Therefore
\[
[x^r]C(x)^8=e_r+8c_r.
\]
By the definition (10) of \(c_r\), this is
\[
e_r+8\left(\frac{16d_r-e_r}{8}\right)=16d_r.
\]
At degree zero, \([x^0]C(x)^8=c_0^8=1\). Thus equality (9) holds coefficient by coefficient, proving the root lemma.

Finally, apply the root lemma to the integers \(d_n=h_n/(16\cdot3^n)\) supplied by (6). Together with (8), it gives an integral power series \(C(x)\) satisfying
\[
C(x)^8
 =1+16\sum_{n\geq1}d_nx^n
 =\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{h_n}{3^n}x^n.
\]
The equality on the right is interpreted in \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\), via the natural inclusion \(\mathbb Z[[x]]\subseteq\mathbb Q[[x]]\). Therefore the power series
\[
\left(\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{h_n}{3^n}x^n\right)^{1/8}
\]
with constant term \(1\) has integer coefficients, as claimed.
